# Archaeology of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea: Historiography, Material Culture, and State Ideology
## 1\. Introduction: The Intersection of Excavation and Ideology
The archaeology of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) constitutes a distinct and insular tradition within East Asian scholarship. Unlike the archaeological practices observed in much of the contemporary world, where the primary objective is often the reconstruction of the past through empirical data and cross-cultural comparison, the discipline in North Korea is intrinsically linked to the validation of the state's official historiography and the Juche ideology. This report provides an exhaustive analysis of the discipline's history, its methodological frameworks, and its key findings across the Paleolithic, Neolithic, Bronze Age (Gojoseon), Goguryeo, and Koryo periods.

The development of archaeology in North Korea cannot be understood apart from the political context of the post-Korean War era. The state's need to establish legitimacy, both domestically and in competition with South Korea, drove a historiographical shift toward emphasizing the antiquity, continuity, and ethnic homogeneity of the Korean people. This has resulted in a unique theoretical landscape where archaeological data is interpreted to support narratives of independent cultural evolution and the centrality of Pyongyang in the development of East Asian civilization.

Key to this interpretive framework is the rejection of diffusionist theories—which attribute cultural changes to external migrations or influences—in favor of indigenous development models. This report will explore how this "Juche archaeology" manifests in the interpretation of specific sites, from the contested dating of the Komunmoru Paleolithic site to the reconstruction of the Tomb of King Tangun and the denial of the Han Commandery of Lelang. Furthermore, it will examine the notable achievements of North Korean archaeology, particularly the preservation and study of the Goguryeo mural tombs, which have garnered international recognition through UNESCO.

## 2\. Historical Development and Institutional Framework
The trajectory of North Korean archaeology has been shaped by the interplay between the legacy of colonial-era scholarship, the influence of Soviet methodologies, and the eventual dominance of indigenous nationalist ideology.

### 2.1 Pre-Liberation Foundations and the Colonial Legacy
Prior to the introduction of modern archaeological practices in the late 19th century, Korea did not possess a systemic tradition of archaeology; early antiquarian texts were largely uninterested in prehistory. The introduction of the discipline coincided with the expanding influence of the Empire of Japan. During the colonial period (1910–1945), Japanese archaeologists conducted extensive surveys of the peninsula. However, their motivations were often rooted in imperialist objectives, seeking evidence of ancestral links between the Yamato people and ancient Koreans to justify colonial rule, or simply engaging in treasure hunting that led to the looting of significant sites .

Despite this colonial imposition, a generation of Korean scholars emerged who sought to reclaim the national past. Following the division of the peninsula after World War II, the foundations of North Korean archaeology were laid by scholars who had been educated in Europe and Japan, bringing with them rigorous methodological training. Two figures stand out in this formative period: To Yu-ho and Han Hung-su.

To Yu-ho (1905–1982), often revered in early narratives as the "father of North Korean archaeology," studied in Vienna. His European education provided him with a sophisticated understanding of stratigraphic excavation and typological analysis, which he sought to apply to the Korean context . Similarly, Han Hung-su (1909–?), who had spent twelve years in Central Europe (1936–1948) studying archaeology and ethnography in Vienna, Bern, and Freiburg, played a pivotal role. Han had previously organized excavations of dolmen sites during the colonial era and was deeply influenced by the nationalist currents he encountered in Europe, as well as the preservationist ethics of his Czech and Austrian colleagues . Upon his return to North Korea via Moscow, Han taught at Kim Il Sung University and helped establish the early academic infrastructure of the state .

### 2.2 The Post-War Institutionalization
The formal institutionalization of the discipline occurred rapidly after the Korean War. On December 1, 1952, the Academy of Sciences (later the Academy of Social Sciences for humanities disciplines) was established, housing the Institute of Archaeology . This centralized body became, and remains, the primary organization responsible for conducting excavations, publishing research, and managing cultural heritage .

In the early post-war period (1950s–early 1960s), North Korean archaeology was heavily influenced by Soviet advisors. Figures like Terenty Shtykov and Nikolai Lebedev advised the North Korean leadership on implementing a Stalinist regime, which extended to the cultural sphere . The curriculum and research focus initially mirrored Soviet models, emphasizing materialist history and class struggle. However, the seeds of a distinct national approach were already being sown.

### 2.3 The Juche Turn and the Purges
A profound transformation occurred in the mid-1960s as Kim Il Sung consolidated his power and the Juche (self-reliance) ideology became the paramount guiding principle of the state. The academic community faced intense pressure to align with the new political orthodoxy, which increasingly viewed dependence on foreign ideas—whether Western or Soviet—as a threat to national sovereignty .

This ideological shift had severe consequences for the founding generation of archaeologists. Kim Il Sung criticized academics for being too influenced by "bourgeois thought" and "flunkeyism" (subservience to great powers). Consequently, To Yu-ho was purged in 1965 and removed from influence. By 1967, almost all academic work was temporarily halted as the state reorganized its intellectual resources to serve the Juche ideology exclusively . Han Hung-su’s fate remains largely obscure in North Korean records, a common outcome for intellectuals of that era who had foreign ties .

When archaeology re-emerged in the 1970s, it was fundamentally transformed. The new "Juche archaeology" was tasked with providing material evidence for three core tenets:

1. **Chaju (Independence):** The Korean people developed their culture and civilization independently, rejecting interpretations that emphasized Chinese influence or diffusion from the continent . 
2. **Continuity and Antiquity:** The Korean Peninsula has been continuously inhabited by the same ethnic group (the Korean Minjok) since the Paleolithic era . 
3. **Centrality:** Pyongyang and the Taedong River basin were the center of this civilization, serving as one of the cradles of humankind .

### 2.4 Modern Institutional Structure
Today, the Institute of Archaeology under the Academy of Social Sciences and the Faculty of History at Kim Il Sung University remain the primary engines of archaeological research . These institutions orchestrate all excavation projects, ensuring that findings are interpreted within the approved ideological framework. They publish academic journals such as *Choson Kogo Yongu* (Archaeological Study of Korea) and reports like *Palaeolithic Sites of Northern Korea* (2009) .

The educational system reinforces this narrative. Since the implementation of the "First Comprehensive 12-Year Compulsory Education Regulation" in 2013, middle schools exclusively teach the history of "orthodox states," effectively removing any historical ambiguity and widening the historiographical gap between North and South Korea . Prominent modern archaeologists, such as Seo Guktae (Neolithic/Bronze specialist) and Choi Seungtaek (Goguryeo specialist), continue to work within these parameters, producing scholarship that is technically detailed yet ideologically rigid .

## 3\. The Paleolithic Period: Constructing the "Origins"
The investigation of the Paleolithic period is not merely a scientific endeavor in North Korea; it is a "national enterprise" of the highest political importance. The regime views the presence of deep human antiquity on the peninsula as essential for establishing the legitimacy of the Korean nation. Kim Jong Il explicitly instructed that "the presence of the Paleolithic period in Korea is far beyond a simple academic matter; it is a very important matter which is directly related to our nation's perpetual history, in particular, our nation's origin" .

### 3.1 The Komunmoru Site and the Lower Paleolithic
The cornerstone of the North Korean claim to a Lower Paleolithic presence is the Komunmoru (Black Anvil) site, located in Hugu-ri, Sangwon County, near Pyongyang. Excavated in 1966, this cave site yielded stone tools and fossilized animal remains that North Korean scholars argue date back approximately one million years .

Lithic Assemblage and Typology: 
The stone tools recovered from Komunmoru are described as heavy, crude implements made of siliceous limestone and vein quartz. The assemblage includes large flake tools, heavy points, trapezoidal tools, and choppers . North Korean typologists emphasize that these tools were produced by a "hurling technique" followed by direct percussion to form cutting edges, with little secondary retouch . 
Crucially, North Korean scholars argue that these tools represent a distinct technological tradition that developed independently of the Acheulean handaxe tradition found in Africa and Europe. They assert that the "knuckle axe-shaped stone implement" found at the site does not follow a standardized form like the Acheulean handaxe but is nonetheless a "typical tool of a primitive man" . 
Faunal Remains and Dating: 
The dating of Komunmoru relies heavily on biostratigraphy. The cave contained the fossilized bones of 29 animal species, 17 of which are extinct . The fauna includes the thick-jawed deer (Megaloceros pachyosteus) and rhinoceros, indicative of a warmer, humid climate corresponding to the early Middle Pleistocene . Based on this faunal association, North Korean archaeologists date the site to roughly 1 million years ago, placing it firmly in the Lower Paleolithic . This aggressive dating underpins the claim that "apemen" (Homo erectus) inhabited the Taedong River basin at the dawn of human history.

### 3.2 The Evolutionary Sequence and the "Taedong River Culture"
Building on the Komunmoru findings, North Korean archaeology posits a linear, unilineal model of human evolution occurring entirely within the Korean Peninsula. This model rejects the "Out of Africa" theory of replacement, instead favoring a multiregional evolution where the Korean people evolved locally from these early hominids.

The proposed evolutionary sequence is categorized into three stages:

| Stage | North Korean Term | Scientific Equivalent | Representative Sites/Fossils |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Apemen** | *Wonin* | *Homo erectus* | Komunmoru (1M years ago) |
| **Paleoanthropic Man** | *Goin* | Archaic *Homo sapiens* | Ryokpho Man, Tokchon Man, Hwadae Man (300k BP) |
| **Neanthropic Man** | *Shinin* | Modern *Homo sapiens* | Sungnisan Man, Mandal Man, Hwangju Man (Upper Paleolithic) |

Recent Discoveries: 
This narrative is continuously reinforced by new discoveries. In 2020, North Korean media announced the discovery of the Hangmok-ri site in Gangdong County, Pyongyang. Artifacts from this cave were scientifically dated to between 34,000 and 36,000 years ago, placing them in the Upper Paleolithic . North Korean sources claim this site as further evidence of the continuous occupation of the Taedong basin during the critical transition to modern humans, linking the "Shinin" directly to the modern Korean ethnicity . 
The Taedong River Culture Theory: 
In 1998, North Korean scholars formally synthesized these findings into the "Taedong River Culture" (Taedonggang Culture) theory. This theory asserts that the Taedong River basin is one of the world's five independent cradles of ancient civilization, comparable to the Nile, Tigris-Euphrates, Indus, and Yellow River civilizations . This theory was politically expedient, emerging during the "Arduous March" famine and the 50th anniversary of the regime; it served to bolster national pride and internal cohesion by presenting North Korea as a culturally superior and ancient nation .

## 4\. The Neolithic and Bronze Age: Gojoseon and the Myth of Tangun
The transition from the Paleolithic to the Neolithic (Jeulmun) and Bronze (Mumun) periods is framed not as a result of migration or technology transfer from China or Siberia, but as an indigenous acceleration of culture. The central focus of this period is **Gojoseon** (Ancient Korea) and its mythical founder, **Tangun**.

### 4.1 Indigenous Origins of Metallurgy and Agriculture
North Korean archaeological thought strictly denies that bronze metallurgy was introduced to the peninsula from the outside. Instead, it argues for an independent invention of bronze working in the Taedong basin during the late 4th millennium BCE . 
Key artifacts supporting this view include:

* **Pipha-shaped Daggers:** The mandolin-shaped bronze dagger is considered the diagnostic artifact of the Gojoseon state. North Korean scholars map the distribution of these daggers across the Korean Peninsula and the Liaodong region of China to delineate the territorial extent of Ancient Korea . The high concentration of these daggers is used to argue that the political center, Wanggeom-seong, was always located in Pyongyang . 
* **Dolmens:** The Taedong basin is described as having an immense concentration of dolmens (megalithic tombs). While North Hamgyong and Ryanggang provinces have fewer (100–500), the Taedong basin is claimed to have about 14,000 dolmens, including "extra-large" types not found elsewhere . This density is cited as proof of a powerful, centralized state capable of mobilizing massive labor forces.

### 4.2 The Excavation and Reconstruction of the Tomb of King Tangun
The most controversial and politically charged event in North Korean archaeology was the "discovery" of the Tomb of King Tangun. Traditionally, Tangun was regarded as a mythical figure who founded Gojoseon in 2333 BCE. However, Kim Il Sung insisted that Tangun was a real historical person and ordered archaeologists to find his remains .

The Excavation (1993–1994): 
In October 1993, the Academy of Social Sciences announced that they had excavated a tomb on the slope of Mount Taebak in Kangdong County, Pyongyang. The excavation report, titled "Excavation reports of the mausoleum of Dangun," claimed the discovery of the skeletons of a male and a female . 
Dating Controversy: 
To validate the antiquity of the remains, North Korean scientists used electron spin resonance (ESR) dating rather than the more conventional radiocarbon dating. They announced a date of 5011 years ago (±267 years), which conveniently placed the burial around 3000 BCE . This date allowed North Korea to claim that Gojoseon was a contemporary of ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia, and that the Korean nation had a 5,000-year history as a "homogeneous nation" . International scholars strongly suspect the date was manipulated to match the legendary founding date, noting that the artifacts found in the tomb were stylistically from the much later Goguryeo period . 
Political Consecration: 
Following the discovery, a massive reconstruction project was launched. The site was transformed into a monumental ziggurat-style mausoleum, 22 meters high and 50 meters on each side, faced with white stone . The complex includes statues of officials and mythical beasts, serving as a national shrine. Kim Il Sung provided detailed instructions on the restoration, emphasizing that the site should demonstrate the "homogeneity of the nation" and be publicized globally . This project effectively canonized Tangun as the biological ancestor of the North Korean people, with the Kim leadership implicitly positioned as his modern successors.

### 4.3 The Denial of the Lelang Commandery
A critical historiographical battleground involves the **Lelang (Rakrang) Commandery**. Established by the Chinese Han Dynasty in 108 BCE after the conquest of Gojoseon, Lelang is widely accepted by international historians to have been administered from a seat near modern Pyongyang.

The Revisionist Theory: 
North Korean ideology finds the idea of a Chinese colonial administration in the heart of the "sacred" capital region unacceptable. Consequently, North Korean scholars have developed a revisionist theory that:

1. **Displacement:** The "Lelang" mentioned in Chinese chronicles was actually located in the Liaodong region of China, not on the Korean Peninsula . 
2. **Indigenous Kingdom:** The rich archaeological remains in Pyongyang—such as timber-chambered tombs, lacquerware, and seals traditionally attributed to the Chinese commandery—are reinterpreted as belonging to an independent Korean kingdom called **"Rakrang" (Nakrang)**. This kingdom is said to have existed concurrently with the Chinese commandery but was politically distinct . 
3. **The Census Tablets:** In the 1990s and 2000s, crucial evidence emerged in the form of wooden tablets (household registers) from a tomb in Pyongyang. These tablets, dated to 45 BCE, contain detailed census data for Lelang counties . While this would seem to confirm the location of the commandery in Pyongyang, North Korean historian Son Yongjong published analyses arguing that the population statistics on the tablets prove the commandery was located elsewhere, or that the presence was merely diplomatic . This "Juche-oriented" interpretation demonstrates the malleability of archaeological data when it conflicts with state imperatives .

## 5\. The Goguryeo Kingdom: The Martial Ancestor
If Gojoseon provides the biological origin of the nation, the **Goguryeo Kingdom (37 BCE – 668 CE)** provides its spiritual and military template. North Korea identifies itself as the successor to Goguryeo, emphasizing the kingdom's martial prowess, its resistance against Chinese dynasties (Sui and Tang), and its control over vast territories in Manchuria .

### 5.1 The Complex of Goguryeo Tombs (UNESCO World Heritage)
The most significant archaeological legacy of this period is the **Complex of Goguryeo Tombs**, inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2004\. The site comprises over 30 individual tombs, many containing exquisite wall paintings that provide a vivid window into ancient Korean life .

#### 5.1.1 Anak Tomb No. 3
Discovered in 1949 in Anak, South Hwanghae Province, this tomb is one of the most structurally complex and artistically rich sites in the peninsula.

* **Architecture:** The tomb is built of stone and features an entrance, an antechamber, a main chamber, and side chambers with stone pillars, resembling an underground palace . 
* **Murals:** The walls are decorated with vibrant frescoes depicting daily life. The eastern chamber features scenes of a kitchen with meat hanging on hooks, a barn, a carriage shed, and household staff . A massive procession scene depicts 250 figures, including soldiers and musicians, demonstrating the occupant's high status . 
* **The Inscription Controversy:** An ink inscription found in the tomb identifies the occupant as **Dong Shou**, a refugee general from the Chinese state of Former Yan who died in 357 CE. While international scholars accept this, North Korean scholars argue that Dong Shou was merely a vassal and that the tomb's grandeur implies it is the mausoleum of a Goguryeo monarch, likely **King Gogugwon** or **King Micheon**.27 This interpretation minimizes the role of "refugees" in favor of indigenous royal agency.

#### 5.1.2 Tokhung-ri Tomb
Excavated in 1976 in Nampo, this tomb is crucial for its extensive inscriptions and astronomical depictions.

* **Inscriptions:** The tomb contains over 600 Sinograms providing biographical data on the occupant, **Chin**. The inscription states he was a governor of Yuju and died in 408 CE . 
* **Geopolitical Implications:** The reference to "Yuju"—a region historically covering parts of modern Beijing and Hebei—is seized upon by North Korean historians to claim that Goguryeo's administrative reach extended deep into China . 
* **Art:** The ceiling features a sophisticated mural of the Milky Way and constellations, demonstrating advanced astronomical knowledge. The walls depict Chin receiving homage from 13 county governors, reinforcing the narrative of a powerful, centralized bureaucracy .

#### 5.1.3 The Tomb of King Tongmyong
Located in Ryongsan-ri, Pyongyang, this is the mausoleum of Jumong (King Tongmyong), the founder of Goguryeo. The site was extensively "restored" (rebuilt) in the 1990s for political reasons .

* **Significance:** The complex includes the royal tumulus and the graves of loyal vassals. Although the original tomb was looted by Japanese archaeologists in 1941, the site is revered as a patriotic shrine. The UNESCO listing recognizes the site for its "artistic elegance" and as testimony to the burial practices of the region .

### 5.2 The "History War" and Conservation
The archaeology of Goguryeo is the central theater of the "history war" between Korea and China. China's "Northeast Project" (2002) attempted to frame Goguryeo as a regional ethnic minority government of ancient China. In response, North Korea accelerated its efforts to register the Goguryeo tombs with UNESCO to assert "ownership" over the history . 
Conservation remains a challenge. The murals face threats from humidity and microbial growth (white mold). The UNESCO project facilitated rare technical cooperation, with international experts installing monitoring systems in tombs like Anak No. 3 and Susan-ri to permit scientific preservation .

## 6\. The Koryo Period: Manwoldae and Inter-Korean Cooperation
While Goguryeo represents military strength, the **Koryo Dynasty (918–1392)** represents the first unified state on the peninsula (as North Korea rejects Unified Silla as a "incomplete" unification due to Silla's alliance with Tang China). The Koryo capital, **Kaesong**, is located just north of the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), making it a unique venue for cross-border archaeology.

### 6.1 The Manwoldae Palace Excavations (2007–2015)
Manwoldae ("Full Moon Terrace") was the main royal palace of Koryo, burned down during the Red Turban invasions in 1361\. From 2007 to 2015, it was the site of a historic joint excavation project between North and South Korea .

* **Findings:** The joint teams uncovered the palace's unique layout, which does not follow the strict north-south axis of Chinese palaces but adapts to the topography of Mount Songak. This adaptation is interpreted as an expression of "Pungsu" (geomancy) and independent aesthetic sensibility . Thousands of artifacts, including cylindrical celadon ceramics and roof tiles with detailed inscriptions, were recovered . 
* **Significance:** This project was a rare instance where the "shared history" of the Koryo Dynasty allowed for scientific collaboration despite political tensions.

### 6.2 The Metal Movable Type Discovery
In 2015, the joint excavation team announced a potentially world-changing discovery: a piece of metal movable type found at the Manwoldae site .

* **The Claim:** North Korean and some South Korean scholars suggested this type could date to the 12th or early 13th century. If verified, this would predate the Gutenberg Bible (1455) by centuries and potentially even the *Jikji* (1377), the oldest confirmed book printed with metal type . 
* **Debate:** The type was found in a disturbed layer, complicating precise dating. While the National Forensic Service in the South later assessed some related finds as potentially later reproductions or requiring more study, the discovery remains a potent symbol of Korea's claim to be the pioneer of printing technology .

## 7\. Political Usage of Archaeology: Nationalism and Legitimacy
In North Korea, archaeology is never neutral. It is a tool for "Socialist Patriotism" and the consolidation of the regime's legitimacy.

### 7.1 "Kim Il Sung Nation" and Bloodline Nationalism
Since the 1980s, North Korean ideology has evolved from orthodox Marxism-Leninism to a race-based nationalism. The concept of the "Kim Il Sung Nation" defines the North Korean people not just by citizenship, but by a shared, ancient bloodline . Archaeology provides the biological proof for this via the "Taedong River Culture" theory, which asserts a separate, superior evolution of the Korean race . By linking the current leadership to Tangun and the "Apemen" of Komunmoru, the regime claims a mandate to rule that is 5,000 years old.

### 7.2 Anti-Colonial Narratives
Excavation reports frequently emphasize the destruction caused by Japanese "imperialist" archaeologists and tomb raiders. The narrative of "restoring" sites like the Tomb of King Tongmyong is framed as healing the wounds of colonialism and reclaiming national dignity .

## 8\. Conclusion
The archaeology of North Korea is a discipline of stark contrasts. On one hand, it has produced remarkable discoveries—particularly the Goguryeo murals and the Koryo palace architecture—that are genuine treasures of world heritage. The state's investment in museums and preservation, despite economic hardships, underscores the high value placed on cultural heritage.

On the other hand, the field is constrained by the rigid requirements of state ideology. The "Taedong River Culture" theory, the aggressive dating of the Tangun Tomb, and the denial of the Lelang Commandery demonstrate how empirical data is often bent to serve the narrative of "Juche." For the international academic community, engaging with North Korean archaeology requires a careful sifting of data: valuing the descriptive richness of their excavations while critically deconstructing the chronological and interpretive frameworks imposed by the state. Nevertheless, projects like the Manwoldae excavation prove that archaeology remains one of the few viable bridges for engagement between the divided halves of the Korean Peninsula.

The Complex of Goguryeo Tombs site comprises over 30 individual tombs.
Many of the tombs in the Complex of Goguryeo Tombs contain exquisite wall paintings that provide a vivid window into ancient Korean life.
Anak Tomb No. 3 is built of stone.
Anak Tomb No. 3 features an entrance, an antechamber, a main chamber, and side chambers with stone pillars.
Anak Tomb No. 3 resembles an underground palace.
The eastern chamber of Anak Tomb No. 3 features scenes of a kitchen with meat hanging on hooks, a barn, a carriage shed, and household staff.
A massive procession scene in Anak Tomb No. 3 depicts 250 figures, including soldiers and musicians.
The procession scene demonstrates the occupant's high status.
International scholars accept that the occupant of Anak Tomb No. 3 was Dong Shou, a refugee general from the Chinese state of Former Yan who died in 357 CE.
North Korean scholars argue that Dong Shou was merely a vassal.
North Korean scholars argue that the grandeur of Anak Tomb No. 3 implies it is the mausoleum of a Goguryeo monarch, likely King Gogugwon or King Micheon.
The inscription in Tokhung-ri Tomb states that the occupant, Chin, was a governor of Yuju.
The inscription in Tokhung-ri Tomb states that the occupant, Chin, died in 408 CE.
The reference to "Yuju" in Tokhung-ri Tomb is seized upon by North Korean historians to claim that Goguryeo's administrative reach extended deep into China.
Yuju is a region historically covering parts of modern Beijing and Hebei.
The ceiling of Tokhung-ri Tomb features a sophisticated mural of the Milky Way and constellations.
The walls of Tokhung-ri Tomb depict Chin receiving homage from 13 county governors.
The Tomb of King Tongmyong was extensively "restored" (rebuilt) in the 1990s for political reasons.
The Complex of Goguryeo Tombs includes the royal tumulus and the graves of loyal vassals.
The original Tomb of King Tongmyong was looted by Japanese archaeologists in 1941.
The UNESCO listing recognizes the Tomb of King Tongmyong site for its "artistic elegance" and as testimony to the burial practices of the region.
China's "Northeast Project" (2002) attempted to frame Goguryeo as a regional ethnic minority government of ancient China.
In response to China's "Northeast Project", North Korea accelerated its efforts to register the Goguryeo tombs with UNESCO to assert "ownership" over the history.
The Goguryeo murals face threats from humidity and microbial growth (white mold).
The UNESCO project facilitated rare technical cooperation, with international experts installing monitoring systems in tombs like Anak No. 3 and Susan-ri to permit scientific preservation.
Manwoldae ("Full Moon Terrace") was the main royal palace of Koryo.
Manwoldae was burned down during the Red Turban invasions in 1361.
From 2007 to 2015, Manwoldae was the site of a historic joint excavation project between North and South Korea.
The joint teams uncovered the palace's unique layout, which does not follow the strict north-south axis of Chinese palaces but adapts to the topography of Mount Songak.
The adaptation of the palace layout is interpreted as an expression of "Pungsu" (geomancy) and independent aesthetic sensibility.
Thousands of artifacts, including cylindrical celadon ceramics and roof tiles with detailed inscriptions, were recovered from Manwoldae.
In 2015, the joint excavation team announced a potentially world-changing discovery: a piece of metal movable type found at the Manwoldae site.
North Korean and some South Korean scholars suggested this type could date to the 12th or early 13th century.
If verified, this metal movable type would predate the Gutenberg Bible (1455) by centuries.
If verified, this metal movable type would potentially even predate the *Jikji* (1377), the oldest confirmed book printed with metal type.
The metal movable type was found in a disturbed layer, complicating precise dating.
The National Forensic Service in the South later assessed some related finds as potentially later reproductions or requiring more study.
Since the 1980s, North Korean ideology has evolved from orthodox Marxism-Leninism to a race-based nationalism.
The concept of the "Kim Il Sung Nation" defines the North Korean people not just by citizenship, but by a shared, ancient bloodline.
Archaeology provides the biological proof for the "Kim Il Sung Nation" via the "Taedong River Culture" theory.
The "Taedong River Culture" theory asserts a separate, superior evolution of the Korean race.
By linking the current leadership to Tangun and the "Apemen" of Komunmoru, the regime claims a mandate to rule that is 5,000 years old.
The narrative of "restoring" sites like the Tomb of King Tongmyong is framed as healing the wounds of colonialism and reclaiming national dignity.

### [National Scientific and Technological Festival Held](https://www.nkeconwatch.com/2007/05/08/national-scientific-and-technological-festival-held/ "Permanent Link to National Scientific and Technological Festival Held")

Tuesday, May 8th, 2007

**KCNA**

 5/8/2007

The national scientific and technological festival commemorating the 95th birth anniversary of President Kim Il Sung was held from May 3 to 7 at the Three-Revolution Exhibition.

The 22nd festival of this kind took place in the forms of a symposium on latest scientific and technological achievements, a presentation of results of scientific researches, a presentation of achievements in technical innovation and a diagram show.

Officials, scientists, technicians and working people across the country presented achievements, experiences and many scientific and technical data attained in the course of the massive technical innovation movement at local scientific and technological festivals.

At least 570 items of data of scientific and technological results highly appreciated there were made public at 18 sections of the national festival.

During the festival the participants introduced achievements in agriculture and light industry and valuable scientific and technological data helpful to revitalizing the national economy and lifting to a high level the technical engineering of such major fields as IT and nanotechnology, bioengineering and basic sciences and widely swapped experiences.

Five persons carried away special prize and 53 top prize at the festival.

The closing ceremony of the national festival took place on Monday. Present there were Choe Thae Bok, secretary of the C.C., Workers’ Party of Korea, Ro Tu Chol, vice-premier of the Cabinet, Pyon Yong Rip, president of the State Academy of Sciences, and others.

The decision of the jury of the festival was made public at the closing ceremony and the festival cups, medals and diplomas were awarded to those highly appraised. And prize of scientific and technological merits went to seven officials who had given precious help to scientists and technicians and presented materials of new research results to the festival.

A closing speech was made by Pak Yong Sin, secretary of the Central Committee of the Korean General Federation of Science and Technology.

### [Academies](https://www.nkeconwatch.com/2007/04/01/academies/ "Permanent Link to Academies")

Sunday, April 1st, 2007

**[Korea Times](http://search.hankooki.com/times/times_view.php?term=north+korea++&path=hankooki3/times/lpage/opinion/200704/kt2007040116363254140.htm&media=kt)**Andrei Lankov

 4/1/2007

Where is science produced? A typical Western answer would be: “in a university, of course.” Actually, it is not really the case these days, since an average teaching routine at most universities is increasingly incompatible with serious research, so a growing share of research is conducted in the corporateowned or independent research centers supported by industry, and by private and/or government money.

Somewhat surprisingly, the communist world was first in separating pure research from a teaching-oriented university. This was initially a Soviet approach, widely accepted by all communist countries, including North Korea.

Most Communist countries had a special academic body whose staff was responsible solely for conducting scientific research. This body was and is called an Academy of Science. In its original Soviet form it could be best described as a self-governing Ministry of Science and Humanities.

The Soviet Union inherited this institution from the old Russia of the tsars. Historically, in pre-Soviet times, the Academy used to be a prestigious closed club of prominent scholars and scientists.

The Communist government took on its payroll, but the institution retained a lot of its ingrained traditions and established privileges. The Soviet Academy of Science was governed by a council of full members, usually well-known scholars and/or academic administrators, who periodically voted new scientists into their circle. Government interference in the process could be serious, but elections still remained contested.

Full membership was a tenured position that could not be withdrawn, even if the bearer was engaged in acts the authorities did not like. Soviet authorities, incidentally, tolerated a high level of critical expression among academy members.

The academy ran a huge network of research centers that formed the backbone of the Soviet research community: the academy always had the best people and the best equipment.

North Korea acquired its own academy in 1952. The preparations began in spring, and on the 1st of December 1952, the academy was officially established. This date became its official foundation day and is regularly celebrated.

At the time of its foundation, the North Korean Academy of Science included 10 full and 15 candidate members and was responsible for 9 “research institutes” and 43 smaller “research laboratories.” Hong Myng-hi was elected as the first President of the Academy, but this aged man was hardly a good administrator. In all probability, Hong was chosen for his background and longstanding reputation as a leftist intellectual of high integrity. In 1956 he was replaced by Paek Nam-un, a prominent historian and another defector from the South (such defectors were very prominent in the North Korean intellectual circles of the 1950s). Unlike his predecessor, Paek was willing to become a real administrator.

Nowadays, the North Korean academy is a large institution. It runs 40 research institutes, about 200 smaller research centers of various kinds, a factory which produces research equipment and 6 publishing houses which issue books and about 40 periodicals. In 1982 the Academy became a ministry, unlike its Soviet counterpart which always had some trappings of an independent “scientists’ club.” But at the same time, the North Korean Academy never even gave a hint of the intellectual, let alone political, independence which was a hallmark of its Soviet counterpart in earlier times.

In the USSR, academies proliferated in the 1940s and 1950s when minor fields began to lobby the government for permission to acquire an academy of their own. Not least, they were attracted to the prestige associated with the name of an “Academy” (and, of course, leading authorities in their respective fields also wanted to be styled a “full member of such-and-such academy”). Thus, the Academy of Medical Science, the Academy of Agricultural Science and even the Academy of Pedagogical Science were born. Each had its own autonomous network of research centers.

A similar process was witnessed in the DPRK where there are minor academies as well. Following the Soviet example, North Korea established an Academy of Medical Science and an Academy of Agricultural Science. Nothing was heard about pedagogy, but the North did create two academies with no Soviet analogue: the Second Academy of Natural Sciences, responsible for military research; and the Academy of Social Science, responsible for the humanities. In 1992 the minor academies, with the exception of the second scademy, fused with the major Academy of Science, but in 1998 the old Soviet-style structure of one major and a number of minor academies was restored.

In better times, a much-coveted job with an academic research institute provided a North Korean scientist with some equivalent of an ivorytower life. Being a staff member of the academy meant good wages, good rations (in North Korea, the latter was more important than the former) and a lot of prestige. In some cases, especially in the natural sciences, the scientists could be even somewhat protected from ongoing political campaigns. However, over the last 15 years, the positions of the academy and its personnel have undergone a dramatic decline.

### [Anti-Epizootic Vaccine Developed](https://www.nkeconwatch.com/2007/03/02/kcna/ "Permanent Link to Anti-Epizootic Vaccine Developed")

Friday, March 2nd, 2007

KCNA

 3/2/2007

The Veterinary Medicine Institute under the Academy of Agricultural Science has developed an efficient vaccine against swine epizootic disease. It is particularly effective against coli bacillus-caused toxemia.

Once a piglet takes the disease, there are symptoms of facial paralysis and melancholia without eating fodder before dying. It is easily infectious.

It has been known that there is no medicine for the disease but preventive measure.

The scientists of the institute have perfected the vaccine developed over 10 years ago, while the research into the epizootic disease is being deepened in the world.

It has been proved that the vaccine is harmless and can prevent piglets completely from dying of coli bacillus-caused disease.

Also the scientists have established a new vaccination system so as to raise the efficacy of vaccine.

The vaccine production centers built in various parts of the country are mass-producing vaccine for stock-breeding farms and rural households.

### [New Method of Breeding Terrapins Developed](https://www.nkeconwatch.com/2007/02/28/new-method-of-breeding-terrapins-developed/ "Permanent Link to New Method of Breeding Terrapins Developed")

Wednesday, February 28th, 2007

**KCNA**

 2/28/2007

Scientists in the Zoological Institute of the Branch Academy of Biology under the DPRK State Academy of Sciences have proved successful in research into the artificial breeding of terrapins.

The terrapin is efficacious for weaklings and for the treatment of circulatory troubles. The new method shortens the growth period of terrapins to one fourth.

At the end of several-year experiments, they found out raw materials of assorted feed needed for the rapid growth of terrapins and their composition rate, and an effective method for reducing incubation duration by more than ten days compared with the natural conditions.

The productivity of the male terrapins is higher than that of the females. They, basing themselves on this, developed a technique by which they can control the rate of female and male freely.

The scientists also redesigned structures of the terrapin breeding farm to suit the habitation of the terrapins so as to make them grow healthily.

### [Banking steps towards the real world](https://www.nkeconwatch.com/2005/12/12/banking-steps-towards-the-real-world/ "Permanent Link to Banking steps towards the real world")

Monday, December 12th, 2005

**[FDI Magazine](http://www.fdimagazine.com/news/fullstory.php/aid/1492/Steps_towards_the_real_world.html)**

 Stephen Timewell

 12/12/2005

On my journey to Pyongyang a Beijing receptionist remarked that the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) is very much like China was 25 years ago. And as the motorcade of China’s president Hu Jintao passed thousands of flower-waving North Koreans on his visit to the world’s most secretive and politically isolated country at the end of October, he may well have agreed.

Visiting Pyongyang is like going back decades in a time machine, to a land with no advertising, no Nokia, Microsoft or McDonald’s billboards and almost no cars. Impressive grand avenues and massive public monuments dominate the landscape but there is no new construction or shops.

The streets are scrubbed clean by hand and are full of hundreds of orderly people wearing their ‘Great Leader’ badges and walking everywhere. Curiously, bicycles are discouraged because of bad accidents and the government encourages power walking for good health, or so I am told. In a country said to spend 30% of its GDP on defence, there is no visual military presence (or overt police presence) in the capital at all.

The ‘traffic ladies’ standing at major intersections are a welcome replacement for traffic lights but there are precious few cars to direct.

Questions greatly outnumber answers in this capital where visitors are duly dazzled by the spectacular grand mass gymnastics and artistic performance (called Arirang) by almost 70,000 children in the massive 150,000-seat May Day Stadium. But visitors are also aware of serious food shortages and cannot ignore the capital’s tallest building, a magnificent 105-floor pyramid tower with a crane on top, left unfinished many years ago, I was informed, due to financial problems.

**Winds of change**

Whether the DPRK is seen as the last Stalinist communist state or as a Confucian nationalist monarchy or even, as it describes itself, as a “powerful socialist nation”, visitors can feel the winds of change, particularly on the economic front. For more than 50 years the iconic stature of the late ‘Great Leader’ Kim Il Sung and that of his successor son Kim Jong Il have dominated the political landscape; the question going forward is how the country’s dire economic circumstances can be improved and whether the regime has the capability to create the new structures needed.

Pyongyang was playing host not only to Mr Hu but also to an increasing number of foreign delegations and journalists, all keen to understand the trends taking place in probably the last country to have massive pictures of Marx and Lenin hanging outside its Ministry of Trade. For many, however, the current focus is progress in the Six-Party Talks on the nuclear weapons programmes of the DPRK.

In the fourth round of talks in September between the two Koreas, China, Japan, Russia and the US a landmark agreement appeared to have been reached. “All six parties emphasised that to realise the inspectable non-nuclearisation of the Korean Peninsula is the target of the Six-Party Talks,” a joint statement said. “The DPRK promised to drop all nuclear weapons and current nuclear programmes and to get back to the non-proliferation treaty as soon as possible and to accept inspections from the International Atomic Energy Agency.”

At the time of going to press in November a fifth round of talks was expected to move a final agreement closer but detailed negotiations over implementation of the above agreement were not expected to be easy or to be concluded quickly. The DPRK, unsurprisingly, wants some payback, be it light-water reactors from the US or other economic incentives.

The core issue is that the DPRK’s publicly acknowledged plutonium programme, believed to provide enough radioactive material for about six bombs, is probably also the country’s key card in trying to rebuild the economy. Kim Jong Il needs to gain maximum advantage from giving up his nuclear threat, but even then, what does his economy have to offer?

**Information hollow**

For a financial journalist the DPRK represents a serious challenge. Understanding the economy and the banking sector of a country is never easy, but when no data is published by the government or the central bank it becomes significantly more difficult. I knew information was scarce but believed that the two very agreeable government minders, assigned to monitor my every move in my four-day visit, would be able to help me extract a simple list of banks operating in the country. No such luck. Although my visit was welcomed, the central bank (which acts as both the issuing bank and as a fully operational commercial bank in the traditional socialist model) failed to provide the list (or anything else), despite numerous requests.

Although the consensus after several interviews was that around 20 banks of various types exist, I can only vouch for the handful listed here. Clearly the Foreign Trade Bank (FTB) represents a pivotal bank in the financial system and Ko Chol Man, director of the FTB, was keen to explain the peculiarities of the DPRK banking system. “The domestic and foreign exchange settlement systems are completely separate. The central bank deals with the domestic market and money issuance and it also has a commercial banking role; the FTB has complete control over foreign exchange matters and trade and also holds the country’s foreign exchange reserves.”

Unlike other banking systems, the FTB in the DPRK acts as a clearing house for the foreign exchange activities of the banks in the country. It does not report to the central bank but, like all banks, reports to the State Fiscal and Financial Committee (SFFC), the overall banking regulator.

Mr Ko was pleased to note that the FTB had around 500 correspondent banks worldwide and, along with its 600 staff (including 11 branches) in North Korea, had six representative offices outside the country (including offices in Austria, Russia and China) and planned to establish a UK representative office in London. However, when asked for details of FTB’s banking activities he replied bluntly that no banking institution had published its figures in terms of activities or balance sheet. “We cannot give figures about the size of our assets because it is a regulation of the state. If the situation becomes better we can make them public but up to now it is impossible.”

**Economic estimates**

Despite the absence of official economic and banking data, various estimates help make the picture a little less murky. A recent Standard Chartered Bank report places North Korea’s nominal GDP at the end of 2004 at $22bn or $957 in GDP per capita terms for the country’s 23 million population; by comparison, South Korea’s nominal GDP is put at $680bn or $14,167 per capita for its 48 million population. While the unification of the two Koreas is seen as an important political objective, especially in Pyongyang, the startling economic gap between the two states could mean that the North becomes a huge burden on the South, and Seoul well recognises the economic problems that emerged from the reunification of Germany in the 1990s.

Meanwhile, Jong Msong Pil, of the Institute of Economy at the Academy of Social Science, explained how the economy had declined dramatically from a GDP per capita of $2500 in the mid-1980s to $480 per capita in 2000.

“The big drop was caused by the disappearance of the socialist market worldwide in the early 1990s; the collapse of our socialist barter trade system led to the failure of many enterprises and a decline in living standards,” he said.

Dr Jong noted that, following the hard times of the mid-1990s, the first target of the national economy has been self-reliance. He added that no economic data had been published since 2000. He believed, however, that 10% economic growth occurred in 2004 and, responding to reports from the World Food Programme (WFP) that a third of the population were malnourished, he said the food situation was improving. “In our country, all people have a job so for this reason no one has died of starvation or hunger. Our country is a socialist planned economy so the government takes care of people’s living.”

Acknowledging shortages in the past, Dr Jong said that in October the government had normalised the public food distribution system, which indicated the government was now supplying sufficient food.

Is the DPRK’s food crisis over? Driving around Pyongyang’s spacious avenues (with two minders) there was no visual evidence of malnutrition – but the capital is likely to be much better served than elsewhere. A supermarket was shown but the goods were only available for foreign currency, hardly food for the masses. Cha Yong Sik, deputy director general at the Ministry of Foreign Trade, said the government had not imported food on a commercial basis in 2005, unlike previous years, but neighbouring countries are still providing significant food aid. Richard Ragan, country director of the WFP, said food production in 2005 was up 10%, with cereals up 6.6%. But while the food situation may have improved, the DPRK is said to be still dependent on food aid.

**Trade predictions**

So what are the DPRK’s prospects? Much depends on the outcome of the nuclear negotiations but estimates from the Seoul-based Korea Trade-Investment Promotion Agency (KOTRA) say the DPRK’s trade volume in 2005 is expected to pass $3bn for the first time since the fall of the Soviet Union with the figure likely to reach $4bn if inter-Korean trade is included. Trade with China, the DPRK’s largest trading partner, grew by more than 40% in the first half of 2005, indicating Pyongyang’s growing dependency on Beijing.

Upbeat on trade prospects, Mr Cha explained that the recently opened Tae-an Friendship Glass Factory, built with a $32m donation from the Chinese government, would export 40% of its 300-ton capacity, mainly to Siberia. Also Pyongyang’s first autumn international trade exhibition in October included companies from six European countries, the focus being on the country’s mineral potential rather than its manufacturing abilities, which are a long way off.

As for banks, the group of up to 15 joint venture banks are helping to finance the country’s 150 or so international companies. But do not expect miracles. The latest, Koryo Global Credit Bank, set up in June, is a joint venture between the UK-based Global Group, headed by Hong Kong businessman Johnny Hon, with 70%, and the state-owned Koryo Bank with 30%. Established with a paid-up capital of e10m, KGC Bank is ambitious in its plans to engage the DPRK in trade and commercial relations with the rest of the world, especially Asia, the Middle East and Europe.

KGCB’s first correspondent banking relationship in Europe is with Germany’s Helababank. The bank, the first product of cooperation in the finance field between the DPRK and the UK, has a staff of five and is also interested in investing in property. It was also able to produce, at the instigation of US authorities, a comprehensive anti-money laundering file.

Another local venture is North East Asia Bank (NEAB), which was set up by ING Group in 1995 but is now wholly owned by the Korean BOHOM Group. Amazingly, Kim Hyon Il, NEAB’s president, produced a balance sheet showing total assets of e79m at the end of 2004 and a paid-up capital of e25m. He also showed me the bank’s newest product, a chip-based cash/debit card, the first in the DPRK. The card demonstrates perhaps that the country is slowly joining the real world – but with only 100 issued and only 13 outlets available, the service has a long way to go.

**Political effects**

 At Daedong Credit Bank, chief executive Nigel Cowie explained how international politics can have a dramatic impact on banking even in the isolated DPRK. In September, just before the conclusion of the fourth round of the Six-Party Talks, the US Treasury accused Banco Delta Asia (BDA), a Macao-based bank, of aiding the DPRK in a series of ‘money laundering’ cases. The Wall Street Journal had said the Macao crackdown was Washington’s method of cutting off Pyongyang’s financial sources for its nuclear weapons programme.

Mr Cowie, a former HSBC banker, explained that all DPRK banks had accounts with BDA for the purposes of remitting funds and, as a result, the accounts were suspended pending an inquiry in mid-November. While Stanley Au, chairman of BDA’s parent, denied the US allegations and BDA’s involvement in any illegal business relations with DPRK banks, the damage is done. “It affects our customers because it affects people’s ability to remit money to and from the country. I imagine that this will cause people doing legitimate business to give up,” says Mr Cowie.

The nuclear negotiations remain critical to the country’s future and the Chinese, in particular, want them to succeed. But that is just a start. There is evidence that the DPRK is opening up and changing with reports that there are 300 open markets operating across the country, 30 in Pyongyang. But whether the DPRK follows the China model of 25 years ago and can restructure its ‘powerful socialist nation’ doctrine remains doubtful under the current leadership.

4.title: Academy of Sciences of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea
4.content:
From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Academy of Sciences of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea[![Image 1: Logo for the State Academy of Sciences of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/94/DPRK_State_Academy_of_Sciences_Logo.png/250px-DPRK_State_Academy_of_Sciences_Logo.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:DPRK_State_Academy_of_Sciences_Logo.png)
Established 1 December 1952; 73 years ago
President[Jang Chol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jang_Chol "Jang Chol")
Staff 50,000
Formerly called National Academy of Sciences
Location Wasan-dong, Podunamu Street, [Sosong District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sosong_District "Sosong District")

, 

[Pyongyang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyongyang "Pyongyang")

, 

[North Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Korea "North Korea")[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-Martino2013-1)

Academy of Sciences of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea
[Chosŏn'gŭl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hangul "Hangul")조선민주주의인민공화국과학원[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-2)
[Hancha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanja "Hanja")朝鮮民主主義人民共和國科學院
[Revised Romanization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revised_Romanization_of_Korean "Revised Romanization of Korean")_Joseon Minjujuui Inmin Gonghwaguk Gwahagwon_
[McCune–Reischauer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCune%E2%80%93Reischauer "McCune–Reischauer")_Chosŏn Minjujuŭi Inmin Konghwaguk Kwahagwŏn_

The **Academy of Sciences of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea** ([Korean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_language "Korean language"): 조선민주주의인민공화국과학원) or **State Academy of Sciences**,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-choson-20160312-3) formerly the **National Academy of Sciences**, is the national [academy of sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_sciences "Academy of sciences") of [North Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Korea "North Korea").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoare201236-4) It was founded in 1952, and until 1981 was responsible for all research conducted in the country before various organizational reforms led to the restructuring of academic facilities. It continues to be a prominent centre for scientific research and education in the country.

The Academy played a role in the [nuclear weapons program of North Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_weapons_program_of_North_Korea "Nuclear weapons program of North Korea") until a separate military-run [Academy of National Defense Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Defence_Sciences "Academy of Defence Sciences") was established to take on this role. Within the academy there are many branches and departments which look after individual domains such as physics, biology, economics, chemistry, history, engineering and mathematics.

Preparations to establish the Academy began in the spring of 1952,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-Lankov2007-5) and the Academy was founded on 1 December 1952.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoare2012xxxi-6) When the Academy was founded, it had 10 full and 15 candidate members in nine research institutes alongside 43 smaller research laboratories. Its first president was Hong Myng-hi, who according to [Andrei Lankov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrei_Lankov "Andrei Lankov"), was not a skilled administrator and chosen for his political loyalty. Hong was followed by Paek Nam-un, who was considered to be more adept.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-Lankov2007-5)

The Academy initiated the [nuclear weapons program of North Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_weapons_program_of_North_Korea "Nuclear weapons program of North Korea") when in 1955 it sent representatives to a conference on peaceful uses of [nuclear power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_power "Nuclear power") in [Eastern Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Europe "Eastern Europe").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMinnich2008260-7) By the late 1950s, the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") was giving practical training in nuclear research to institutions affiliated with the North Korean Academy of Sciences. In 1957, the Soviets dispatched [I. M. Gramenitsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=I._M._Gramenitsky&action=edit&redlink=1 "I. M. Gramenitsky (page does not exist)") to teach the Academy about thick-layered [emulsion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emulsion "Emulsion") in nuclear physics.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZhebin201130-8) In 1959, North Korea struck a deal with the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") on setting up a nuclear research facility under the Academy near [Yongbyon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongbyon "Yongbyon").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEArrigoni1994254-9)

A parallel development in the late 1950s was the purging of intellectuals unfavorable to [Kim Il Sung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Il_Sung "Kim Il Sung") from the Academy in 1957. In the aftermath of the [August Faction Incident](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/August_Faction_Incident "August Faction Incident") that sought to oust Kim the previous year, a meeting to uncover and punish "factionalists" was organized at the Academy from August to November 1957.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTELankov200298-10) One of those purged was [Yi Chong-won](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yi_Chong-won&action=edit&redlink=1 "Yi Chong-won (page does not exist)"), "one of the founding fathers of Korean Marxist historiography".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTELankov200297-11)

In the 1970s, a number of State Academy of Sciences institutes were moved from [Pyongyang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyongyang "Pyongyang") to the city of [Pyongsong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyongsong "Pyongsong"), some 50 kilometres (31 mi) outside of the capital. The headquarters of the Academy remained in the Sosong District in central Pyongyang. There are now 17 such research institutions in Pyongsong, all of them part of the network of the Academy of Sciences.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDenisov201123-12)

According to Lankov, the Academy does not exhibit "a hint of the intellectual, let alone political, independence" that academies in other countries, including the [Soviet Academy of Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Academy_of_Sciences "Soviet Academy of Sciences") at times, have.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-Lankov2007-5)

On 11 January 1999, [North Korean leader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Korean_leader "North Korean leader")[Kim Jong Il](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Jong_Il "Kim Jong Il") chose the Academy as his first location of [on-the-spot guidance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On-the-spot_guidance "On-the-spot guidance") of the year, which he had declared the "year of sciences". According to Sung Chull Kim, "[i]t is unquestionable that this visit was more than a symbolic gesture" relating to Kim's strategy of prioritizing the information technology industry.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-Kim2012-13)

The Academy is the most important scientific institution in the country, hence being quite large in terms of facilities as well as staff.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoare201236-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-Lankov2007-5)

The Academy directly reports to the [Cabinet of North Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_North_Korea "Cabinet of North Korea"), the supreme administrative body of the DPRK.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoare201236-4) Under the Academy, there are various organizations and six publishing houses,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoare201236-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-Lankov2007-5) including the Academy of Sciences Publishing House in the [Central District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_District_(Pyongyang) "Central District (Pyongyang)") of [Pyongyang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyongyang "Pyongyang").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-ZimKorEu-14) The Academy issues books and some 40 periodicals.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-Lankov2007-5)_[Kwahakwon Tongbo](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kwahakwon\_Tongbo&action=edit&redlink=1 "Kwahakwon Tongbo (page does not exist)")_ ([Korean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_language "Korean language"): 과학원통보, Korean for 'Bulletins of the Academy of Sciences'), is the organ of its standing committee and is published six times a year.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-ZimKorEu-14) Affiliated with the Academy, there are institutions dealing with various fields including [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics "Mathematics"), [physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physics "Physics"), [chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemistry "Chemistry"), [engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engineering "Engineering"), [medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicine "Medicine"), [law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law "Law"), [economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economics "Economics"), [history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History "History"), [literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literature "Literature"), [philology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philology "Philology"), [ethnography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnography "Ethnography") and [archaeology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology "Archaeology"). A [biology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biology "Biology") research laboratory is under its direct control.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-Kim2003-15) Although there is a separate [Academy of Social Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Academy_of_Social_Sciences_(North_Korea)&action=edit&redlink=1 "Academy of Social Sciences (North Korea) (page does not exist)")([ko](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EC%82%AC%ED%9A%8C%EA%B3%BC%ED%95%99%EC%9B%90 "ko:사회과학원")), there are several [social science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_science "Social science") institutes attached to the Academy of Sciences. Various committees work on [linguistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linguistics "Linguistics"), the compilation of classics,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoare201236-4) the compilation of technical terms, and language reform.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-Kim2003-15) An [Academy of Koryo Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Academy_of_Koryo_Medicine&action=edit&redlink=1 "Academy of Koryo Medicine (page does not exist)") was founded under the Academy of Sciences in 1962 to study [traditional Korean medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traditional_Korean_medicine "Traditional Korean medicine").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoare2012244-16)

The Academy Headquarters is based in the [Sosong District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sosong_District "Sosong District") of Pyongyang, the capital of North Korea.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-Martino2013-1)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoare201236-4) While some facilities of the Academy are located in Pyongyang, much of its activities actually take place in Pyongsong.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoare201236-4) Many Academy facilities are located in Pyongyang's [Unjong District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unjong_District "Unjong District"),[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-17) a district that lies in between the capital city's center and the city of Pyongsong. Pyongyang retains branches involved in the research of biology, construction, building materials, electronics and automation, and light industry.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-Corfield2014-18) A branch exists in [Hamhung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamhung "Hamhung"), [South Hamgyong Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Hamgyong_Province "South Hamgyong Province").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoare201236-4)

Between 1994 and 1998 it was briefly renamed as the National Academy of Sciences.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-Lankov2007-5) On 5 September 1999, the Academy merged with the State Commission for Science and Technology.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-ICSU-19) Since the 1980s, the Academy has suffered from the lack of funds,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoare201236-4) and since the early 1990s, it and its personnel have experienced "a dramatic decline" in standing. Before that, positions in the Academy were much sought-after and could provide good wages, rations, and prestige.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-Lankov2007-5)

The Academy maintains websites, but they are only accessible through the [North Korean Intranet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Korean_Intranet "North Korean Intranet").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKoJangLee2008246-20)

All science on the highest level was conducted by the single Academy of Sciences until 1981, when it was split into separate affiliate academies; namely the Academy of Social Sciences, [Academy of Agricultural Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Academy_of_Agricultural_Sciences_of_North_Korea&action=edit&redlink=1 "Academy of Agricultural Sciences of North Korea (page does not exist)"), [Academy of Medical Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Academy_of_Medical_Sciences_of_North_Korea&action=edit&redlink=1 "Academy of Medical Sciences of North Korea (page does not exist)"), [Academy of Light Industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Academy_of_Medical_Sciences_of_North_Korea&action=edit&redlink=1 "Academy of Medical Sciences of North Korea (page does not exist)"), and the original Academy of Sciences.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTESeekins198192-21) In 1992 the minor academies were merged with the Academy of Sciences, only to be split off again in 1998. A [Second Academy of Natural Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Academy_of_Natural_Sciences "Second Academy of Natural Sciences"), tasked with [military science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_science "Military science"), remains separate from the main Academy.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-Lankov2007-5)

The Academy currently has 40 research institutes and 200 smaller research centers.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-Lankov2007-5) It has 50,000 employees.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-Madden2013-22) Its current president is [Jang Chol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jang_Chol "Jang Chol"),[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-23) who was preceded by [Pyon Yong-rip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyon_Yong-rip "Pyon Yong-rip").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-Martino2013-1) The Academy is a member of the [International Council for Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Council_for_Science "International Council for Science") since 1961.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-ICSU-19)

The Academy operates a [Special Economic Zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Economic_Zone "Special Economic Zone") near Unjong Park in the northern suburbs of [Pyongyang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyongyang "Pyongyang").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People's_Republic_of_Korea#cite_note-24)
